newsitem.title: USA: Lee Kuan Yew gives U.S. advice on China.
newsitem.headline: Lee Kuan Yew gives U.S. advice on China.

text.p: The father of modern Singapore has called on the United States to help China integrate into the world community through a new strategic understanding.

Lee Kuan Yew, who holds the title of senior minister after 31 years as Singapore's prime minister, said the key to such a Sino-U.S. understanding was U.S. policy on the future of Taiwan. "China will pay any price to prevent Taiwan breaking away," Lee said in a speech late on Monday accepting the 1996 "Architect of the New Century" award from the non-partisan Nixon Centre for Peace and Freedom.

"The only country with the capability to help Taiwan in any bid for separate independence is America," he said. "A major cause for instability will be removed if China believes that America is not helping Taiwan to split away."

Lee, introduced at the $1,000-a-plate fund-raising dinner in glowing terms by former Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, urged the United States to "use the time available" to encourage China's communist leaders to play a part in shaping the post-Cold War international order.

"Then China will find it worthwhile to accept its obligations as a global citizen. China will slowly understand that integration with other major economic powers will be much more beneficial than going it alone and trying to extend its sphere of influence. The old Soviet Union tried the other course and failed," he said.

"America and China need to reach a new strategic understanding," he added, saying China should be brought into the World Trade Organisation "after a short period of transition as a developing country."

"The world will not be better off with a China that is not bound by its rules," Lee said. He hailed President Bill Clinton's 1993 decision "de-linking" Beijing's human rights record from the annual U.S. decision on whether to grant China normal trading status, calling it "an important advance in the right direction."

Lee, 73, an authoritarian leader who formally handed over the reins of power in 1990, made no public comment about the controversy that erupted over the Nixon Center's decision to award him its second annual Architect of the New Century award. The first went to House Speaker Newt Gingrich.

Last month, New York Times columnist William Safire, an old nemesis, slammed the decision to honour Lee as "sucking up to a tinpot tyrant with dynastic pretentions." Safire called on "all good Nixonites" to skip a dinner honouring a "dictator who despises a free press and individual liberty."

But Kissinger and other Nixon loyalists turned out in big numbers, including former CIA directors James Schlesinger and Richard Helms and former Secretary of State Alexander Haig. The centre was founded by former President Richard Nixon shortly before his death in 1994.

Lee said Nixon, "a pragmatic strategist," would have sought to engage, not contain, China. "But he would also quietly set pieces into place for a fallback position should China not play accordiing to the rules of a good global citizen."
This meant keeping the friendship of key players in East Asia as well as Russia, "for in 30 years Russia may again be on the march," Lee said.
